svg.title: Discard edits in one working file.
svg.desc: Restoring a working file replaces its saved contents. Requires Git 2.23 or newer, inside a repository with an existing committed, tracked note.txt. HEAD means the last commit. In this example both HEAD and staging contain hello; an unstaged working edit adds again. First back up the file and inspect git diff -- note.txt. git restore --source=HEAD -- note.txt explicitly copies the last committed version into that working file, erasing its uncommitted working edits. Git cannot undo edits it never recorded. A diagram shows hello and again becoming only hello while staging and commits remain unchanged. Plain git restore without --staged instead copies from staging, which does not always match HEAD. Only the chosen tracked path is addressed, not untracked files or history rewriting. Contents are illustrative.
svg.text: GIT HISTORY / 05
DISCARD EDITS IN ONE WORKING FILE.
git restore replaces a working file's contents with a selected saved version.
Git 2.23+; inside a repository with a committed, tracked note.txt.
HEAD = last commit. Staging (next commit's selected files) matches it here.
Back up first. Inspect the unstaged edit: git diff -- note.txt
WARNING: erases this file's uncommitted working edits.
No Git undo for edits it never recorded. Restore only the chosen path:
git restore --source=HEAD -- note.txt
Example note.txt contents: only the working file you edit was changed.
Working: before
after
Staging + commit
hello
again
hello
hello
unchanged
Plain git restore without --staged copies staging to the working file,
not always the last commit. Above, --source=HEAD chooses that commit explicitly.
